title: Complement of quantum approximate counting in \(\mathrm{QMA}(2)\)
formal: Is the following complementary quantum approximate-counting promise problem in \(\mathrm{QMA}(2)\)? The input is a finite quantum verification circuit \(V\) with \(w\) witness qubits, together with a binary integer \(1\le K\le2^w\). Let \(A_V\) be its acceptance operator on the witness space and let \(D_a(V)\) count its eigenvalues at least \(a\), with multiplicity. Distinguish \[\text{YES: }D_{1/3}(V)\le K/2\qquad\text{from}\qquad\text{NO: }D_{2/3}(V)\ge K,\] promised that one of these conditions holds. Membership asks for one uniform polynomial-time quantum verifier using two polynomial-size, mutually unentangled witnesses, with completeness at least \(2/3\) and soundness at most \(1/3\). The two spectral thresholds deliberately leave a buffer; the selected target is the complement of this buffered counting problem.
why: This asks whether two unentangled quantum certificates can verify that a quantum verifier has only a small accepting space. It connects the power of independent quantum witnesses to approximate counting and distinguishes proving scarcity from merely proving existence.

sentences: The selected task asks whether two unentangled quantum witnesses can certify a small accepting eigenspace.
The input is an explicitly described quantum verification circuit and a binary threshold for its spectral count.
A low count at acceptance threshold one third must be distinguished from a count at least twice as large at threshold two thirds.
The spectral buffer permits intermediate eigenvalues and avoids treating the source’s shortened one-threshold description as the full model.
The target is ordinary QMA(2) membership of the complementary promise problem; known quantum-oracle lower bounds concern different models.

definitions:
Use a conventional explicit binary circuit encoding. It specifies the ordered list of gates and their wire indices, which wires hold the \(w\) input witness qubits, which \(a\ge1\) ancillary qubits start in \(|0\rangle\), and one measured output wire. Wire counts are written in unary, so both \(w\) and \(a\) are bounded by the input length. The allowed gates are the fixed exact unitary matrices \[H=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\quad T=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&e^{i\pi/4}\end{pmatrix},\quad \mathrm{CNOT}|b,c\rangle=|b,b\oplus c\rangle,\] acting as identity on the other wires. Here \(b,c\in\{0,1\}\), \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two, and \(i^2=-1\). The sole measurement of \(V\) is its final computational-basis output, with value one interpreted as acceptance. The input includes the complete gate list, not an oracle or a succinct generator of an exponentially long circuit. Let \(N\) be the total bit length of the circuit description and the binary encoding of \(K\). Malformed inputs and inputs outside the promise have no correctness requirement. The bound \(K\) varies with the input and may be exponential in \(w\); it is not a universal constant.

A state of the witness register is a density matrix \(\rho\) on \(\mathbb C^{2^w}\): a Hermitian positive semidefinite matrix of trace one. Hermitian means \(\rho=\rho^\dagger\), and positive semidefinite means \(v^\dagger\rho v\ge0\) for every complex vector \(v\). With \(\Pi_1\) the projector onto output one, define \[A_V=(I\otimes\langle0^a|)V^\dagger\Pi_1V(I\otimes|0^a\rangle).\] It satisfies \(0\preceq A_V\preceq I\) and \(\Pr[V\text{ accepts }\rho]=\operatorname{Tr}(A_V\rho)\). Its \(2^w\) eigenvalues lie in \([0,1]\). For \(a\in[0,1]\), \(D_a(V)=\operatorname{rank}\mathbf1_{[a,1]}(A_V)\): the dimension of the span of eigenvectors with eigenvalue at least \(a\). Eigenvalues are counted with multiplicity, including equality at the threshold. This is neither the number of individual normalized states nor the dimension of an arbitrarily chosen accepting basis. There are continuously many possible witnesses, but the spectral count is a finite integer.

Since \(D_{1/3}\ge D_{2/3}\) and \(K>0\), the two promised cases are disjoint. The YES bound means \(D_{1/3}\le\lfloor K/2\rfloor\). Eigenvalues strictly between \(1/3\) and \(2/3\) are allowed; the promise does not say the entire spectrum avoids this interval. They contribute to the larger count, but not the smaller one. The uncomplemented buffered counting problem labels \(D_{2/3}\ge K\) as YES and \(D_{1/3}\le K/2\) as NO. Complementation swaps these two sets and retains the promise; it does not replace \(A_V\) by \(I-A_V\) or count all eigenvalues below a single threshold.

For \(\mathrm{QMA}(2)\), there must exist one deterministic classical polynomial-time circuit generator and a fixed polynomial \(p\) such that, on every input \(x=(V,K)\) of length \(N\), it produces a circuit \(W_x\) with at most \(p(N)\) gates and private zero-initialized ancilla qubits. Two additional witness registers \(R_1,R_2\) each have at most \(p(N)\) qubits. Their supplied joint state must have the form \(\rho_1\otimes\rho_2\); each factor may itself be mixed and internally entangled, with arbitrary complex entries and no efficient-preparation requirement. The verifier may act jointly on the two registers and its ancillas, using the gate convention above, and measures a final output bit. Write its acceptance probability as \(p_x(\rho_1,\rho_2)\). The requirements are \[x\in L_{\mathrm{yes}}\Rightarrow\exists\rho_1,\rho_2:\ p_x(\rho_1,\rho_2)\ge2/3,\] \[x\in L_{\mathrm{no}}\Rightarrow\forall\rho_1,\rho_2:\ p_x(\rho_1,\rho_2)\le1/3.\] Product witnesses suffice to specify soundness; by linearity the same bound then holds for every separable mixture of products. Soundness is not required against arbitrary entangled states across the two supplied registers. There are no additional messages, advice or oracle calls. Polynomial running time is measured in \(N\), including the length of \(K\), not in its numerical value or in \(2^w\). The spectral count describes the problem; no eigenbasis is supplied to the verifier.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked proof that this exact promise pair belongs to \(\mathrm{QMA}(2)\), or a complete Lean-checked proof that it does not. An affirmative answer must supply a uniform verifier with polynomial resources and prove both quantified acceptance conditions for all promised circuit inputs and all allowed witnesses. A negative answer must rule out every such verifier, rather than one proposed protocol. A result for a single spectral threshold, a verifier given an eigenbasis, exponentially large witnesses, entangled witnesses without the stated product restriction, or a model with interaction or an oracle does not establish the claim. Quantum-oracle separations alone do not give an unrelativized nonmembership theorem. This is an exact class-membership question; the fixed counting promise and verifier error are part of the model, not a request to estimate a number to additive precision.

context_blocks.text: The imported card broadly asked for the complexity of quantum approximate counting. The source separately asks whether its complement is in QMA(2). On 16 September 2026 the user selected that narrower target and authorized repairing the brief single-threshold description to the standard version with two separated spectral thresholds. This scope change is explicit; the broad classification programme is not claimed complete.

An ordinary quantum witness can demonstrate the existence of a state that a verifier accepts. Approximate counting asks how large the accepting eigenspace is. The selected complement instead asks for efficient verification that even the lower-threshold accepting space is small.

Definition 17 of the ITCS 2026 paper uses two thresholds \(b<a\) separated by at least an inverse polynomial, and allows a returned estimate between \((1-\varepsilon)D_a\) and \((1+\varepsilon)D_b\). The present decision formulation fixes the spectral thresholds to \(2/3\) and \(1/3\) and keeps the original source's factor-two count gap. It does not assume an absence of eigenvalues between the thresholds.

The two witnesses in QMA(2) are separate resources. They may be compared by a joint quantum verifier, but cannot arrive entangled with one another. The requested membership is therefore different from supplying one larger arbitrary witness, and from asking two provers to participate in an interactive protocol.

The ITCS 2026 authors prove a quantum-oracle separation between quantum approximate counting and quantum verification with a QMA oracle, ruling out a black-box analogue of the classical approximate-counting algorithm in that setting. Their statement concerns an additional oracle and a different verification model. It does not settle this ordinary two-witness complement question.

The phrase quantum approximate counting also occurs for counting marked inputs of a classical Boolean oracle using quantum queries, or for estimating the acceptance probability of a computation with no witness. The cited paper explicitly distinguishes those tasks from counting the accepting eigenspace of a quantum verifier.
